old: ZERO SEPARABILITY (D12.3): satisfied. These are mutually exclusive employment-STATUS categories, not intensity bands: every category containing positive paid work (full-time, part-time, self-employed) is separate from every category containing no paid work (unemployed, retired), so there is no residual band pooling zero work with low-intensity work. Contrast rautio2016, where the '<25.0%' band made paid_any unidentifiable. SELF-EMPLOYMENT is counted as paid work; the sibling cohort's own review literature and nossel2018's definition both treat self-employment as paid employment. It is not counted as competitive because this report establishes no labour-market setting. DENOMINATOR: n_outcome_observed = 16311, the printed 16,862 minus the printed 551/501 with missing employment data. reported_percentage_base = 16,862 because the authors' own percentages divide by the full matched cohort including the missing category (12,721/16,862 = 75.4 exactly, as printed). NO HORIZON: followup_basis = unclear and followup_months is left blank. The outcome is 'based on the most recent nonmissing data during the study period', the study period runs 1 January 2013 to 30 September 2019 and includes the 12-month pre-index baseline, and the authors state that 'because a cross-sectional approach was used in examining societal outcomes across the full study period, no temporality was applied between the exposure (relapse) and the outcomes of interest'. Mean follow-up was 4.7 years but that is the length of the observation window, not the time at which employment was measured, so no elapsed time from cohort entry can be assigned and no landmark horizon applies. ARM: this is a propensity-score-matched relapse subgroup of the 119,343-veteran schizophrenia cohort, not a whole recruited cohort, so it cannot enter the primary prevalence estimand (SAP 2.1 and 7) irrespective of the conflict status. MODERATOR: only the male count is printed (15,499 of 16,862); the sex variable is not shown to be exhaustive, so n_female is left blank rather than derived by complement.

new: The trial prospectively registered and published protocol/SAP/HEAP; the source alone does not permit a complete comparison against their specified socio-occupational analyses. The altered Cox model concerns disengagement, not these outcomes; absence of arm means or a P value is incomplete reporting and does not itself demonstrate selective reporting.

new: The trial prospectively registered and published protocol/SAP/HEAP; the source alone does not permit a complete comparison against their specified socio-occupational analyses. Some concerns therefore remains provisional. The altered Cox model concerns disengagement, not these outcomes; absence of arm means or a P value is incomplete reporting and does not itself demonstrate selective reporting.

This supports the operational annual main-employment construct; it does not establish any-work point prevalence.

new: The frame broadens beyond clinical services using community screens and self-reported psychotic symptoms, but those methods do not establish psychotic-disorder diagnoses for roughly half the recruitment. old: The frame is the non-institutionalised adult population aged 18 or older living in one university-hospital catchment area, a typical mixed commercial and residential urban area north of Bangkok. The authors deliberately went beyond service records to reach people never in contact with services, on the stated ground that 'a substantial number of psychotic patients have no previous or current contact with psychiatric services, it is therefore essential to identify and include such groups of patients in the study to maximize the inclusiveness and representativeness of the psychotic patient population'. For a prevalence estimand this is better than a clinic frame, and it is one of very few cohorts in the review that reaches untreated cases.
new: The frame broadens beyond clinical services using community screens and self-reported psychotic symptoms, but those methods do not establish psychotic-disorder diagnoses for roughly half the recruitment. Applicability to the target diagnosed-psychosis population is therefore uncertain even though the catchment itself is well defined.

old: Only 277 of the 551 recruited, about half, have a stated diagnostic criterion, being a treated ICD-10 F20-F29 diagnosis in hospital or primary care records. The remaining 274 were identified by a psychosis screening questionnaire administered by community key informants or by a self-reported lifetime history of psychotic symptoms in an earlier survey, and the WMH-CIDI was used to assess 'history of psychotic symptoms and service utilization' rather than to make a diagnosis. Screening positive for psychotic symptoms is not the same as having a psychotic disorder, and no confirmation step is reported for the community-identified half, so the proportion of the cohort with a qualifying psychosis diagnosis sits within a percentage point of the review's 50% threshold.
new: Item 6 concerns employment. Employment is explicitly defined as any self-reported personal earnings in the prior 12 months from wages/employment stipends, excluding pensions, investment and other assistance. This gives a valid operational paid-work identification rule. Diagnostic uncertainty belongs to population eligibility/frame, not this outcome item.

old: Participants, the vocational specialist, the study lead and the participants' case managers all knew the allocation; only the research assistants were masked. Only four participants did not complete the intervention. The more substantial concern is contamination of the control condition by the trial itself: the authors' own leading explanation for an unusually high control-arm employment rate (48% against 9.5% in their earlier trial at the same clinic) is a change in clinical culture, with workshops that upskilled EPPIC clinicians in helping clients obtain work and one clinical post converted to an IPS post. That is a deviation arising from the trial context that would attenuate the estimated effect of assignment. The analysis was modified intention-to-treat, including only participants with at least one post-randomisation assessment, so 15 randomised participants are outside it.
new: Participants and clinicians were unmasked, but no differential deviations arising from participation in this trial are established. The workshops and clinical IPS-post conversion occurred in the two-year interval BEFORE this trial, following the earlier RCT, and describe background usual-care evolution rather than current-trial contamination. Excluding participants without observed outcomes belongs principally to the missing-data domain. These facts do not justify the original escalation above low for an assignment effect.

old: Participants, the vocational specialist, the study lead and the participants' case managers all knew the allocation; only the research assistants were masked. Only four participants did not complete the intervention. The more substantial concern is contamination of the control condition by the trial itself: the authors' own leading explanation for an unusually high control-arm employment rate (48% against 9.5% in their earlier trial at the same clinic) is a change in clinical culture, with workshops that upskilled EPPIC clinicians in helping clients obtain work and one clinical post converted to an IPS post. That is a deviation arising from the trial context that would attenuate the estimated effect of assignment. The analysis was modified intention-to-treat, including only participants with at least one post-randomisation assessment, so 15 randomised participants are outside it.
new: Participants and clinicians were unmasked, but no differential deviations arising from participation in this trial are established. The workshops and clinical IPS-post conversion occurred in the two-year interval BEFORE this trial, following the earlier RCT, and describe background usual-care evolution rather than current-trial contamination. Excluding participants without observed outcomes belongs principally to the missing-data domain. These facts do not justify the original escalation above low for an assignment effect.

old: Both groups are selected subsets of their sites, defined by a non-standardised judgement. In Aarhus 116 of 283 eligible OPUS patients entered Morpheus; in Aalborg a nurse retrospectively identified 130 of 216 as patients who would have been eligible. The authors state that "patient inclusion in Morpheus was not standardised, which made it challenging to identify a comparable population in Aalborg" and that the 60% Aalborg eligibility estimate exceeds the 41% actually treated in Aarhus, so the comparator is defined partly after the fact.
new: The comparison is selected by non-standardised prospective Morpheus assessment versus retrospective identification of potentially eligible controls. Among OPUS patients eligible by age and programme duration,116/283 in Aarhus versus 130/216 in Aalborg were selected. Additionally OPUS participation of 1-2.5 years was required, conditioning entry on post-baseline retention. These factors support serious selection concerns for the intervention effect.

old: Both groups are selected subsets of their sites, defined by a non-standardised judgement. In Aarhus 116 of 283 eligible OPUS patients entered Morpheus; in Aalborg a nurse retrospectively identified 130 of 216 as patients who would have been eligible. The authors state that "patient inclusion in Morpheus was not standardised, which made it challenging to identify a comparable population in Aalborg" and that the 60% Aalborg eligibility estimate exceeds the 41% actually treated in Aarhus, so the comparator is defined partly after the fact.
new: The comparison is selected by non-standardised prospective Morpheus assessment versus retrospective identification of potentially eligible controls. Among OPUS patients eligible by age and programme duration,116/283 in Aarhus versus 130/216 in Aalborg were selected. Additionally OPUS participation of 1-2.5 years was required, conditioning entry on post-baseline retention. These factors support serious selection concerns for the intervention effect.

In Aarhus 116 of 283 eligible OPUS patients entered Morpheus; in Aalborg a nurse retrospectively identified 130 of 216 as patients who would have been eligible. The authors state that "patient inclusion in Morpheus was not standardised, which made it challenging to identify a comparable population in Aalborg" and that the 60% Aalborg eligibility estimate exceeds the 41% actually treated in Aarhus, so the comparator is defined partly after the fact.

Among OPUS patients eligible by age and programme duration,116/283 in Aarhus versus 130/216 in Aalborg were selected. Additionally OPUS participation of 1-2.5 years was required, conditioning entry on post-baseline retention. These factors support serious selection concerns for the intervention effect.

old: The trial is registered as ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03273530, a number in the 2017 series, so registration postdates the 2013-2015 conduct of the trial and no prespecified analysis plan predates the results. Two printed results are not reproducible from the paper's own numbers: p = .002 is reported both for ISE versus TVR, which a two-sided chi-square on 34/54 against 18/54 reproduces, and for ISE versus IPS, which on 34/54 against 27/54 gives approximately p = 0.17; and the text states that 'The ISE group had significantly higher scores on the BPRS, the GAF, and the PWI' when Table 2 shows the ISE group with the LOWEST BPRS score at every follow-up, which on the BPRS means fewer symptoms. The exact test behind each post-hoc comparison is not specified.
new: A ClinicalTrials.gov identifier is cited, but registration timing and the prospective plan were not independently inspected, so prespecification is unverified. The ISE-versus-IPS printedP=.002 does not reproduce from 34/54 versus 27/54 using a simple unadjusted two-sided chi-square test; the exact pairwise procedure is insufficiently described. This is a reporting concern, not proof of selection from multiple eligible analyses. The original claim that ISE has the lowest BPRS at EVERY follow-up is false at 11 months, and symptom reporting does not itself establish selection of this employment result. Some concerns is supported provisionally.

The exact test behind each post-hoc comparison is not specified.
new: A ClinicalTrials.gov identifier is cited, but registration timing and the prospective plan were not independently inspected, so prespecification is unverified. The ISE-versus-IPS printedP=.002 does not reproduce from 34/54 versus 27/54 using a simple unadjusted two-sided chi-square test; the exact pairwise procedure is insufficiently described. This is a reporting concern, not proof of selection from multiple eligible analyses. The original claim that ISE has the lowest BPRS at EVERY follow-up is false at 11 months, and symptom reporting does not itself establish selection of this employment result. Some concerns is supported provisionally.

old: Estimand: the effect of being prescribed antipsychotic medication, versus not being prescribed it, on working at the 20-year follow-up, in a naturalistic non-randomised comparison. The two counts (9 of 36 and 16 of 22) exist in the report only as the two sides of that comparison, which is why ROBINS-I rather than the JBI prevalence checklist is applied: neither count is a whole-cohort prevalence, and neither arm was randomised. This row is the 'prescribed antipsychotics at 20 years' side. Medication status was determined by clinicians and patients, not by the investigators, so confounding by indication is intrinsic: patients who remain on antipsychotics for twenty years differ systematically in illness severity, insight and treatment engagement from those who stop, and the report itself shows that those continuously prescribed antipsychotics were significantly more likely to have negative symptoms, which it also shows predicts not working. The authors address this seriously, with separate analyses controlling for prognostic potential (Vaillant), premorbid developmental achievement (Zigler), psychosis and negative symptoms, and a GEE logistic and proportional-odds model adjusting for prognosis, premorbid functioning and symptoms. Those adjustments are post-hoc, use dichotomised covariates, and cannot address baseline severity determining both medication continuation and work capacity. The specific 20-year comparison reported as 9/36 v. 16/22 is unadjusted.

old: Estimand: the effect of being prescribed antipsychotic medication, versus not being prescribed it, on working at the 20-year follow-up, in a naturalistic non-randomised comparison. The two counts (9 of 36 and 16 of 22) exist in the report only as the two sides of that comparison, which is why ROBINS-I rather than the JBI prevalence checklist is applied: neither count is a whole-cohort prevalence, and neither arm was randomised. This row is the 'not prescribed antipsychotics at 20 years' side. Medication status was determined by clinicians and patients, not by the investigators, so confounding by indication is intrinsic: patients who remain on antipsychotics for twenty years differ systematically in illness severity, insight and treatment engagement from those who stop, and the report itself shows that those continuously prescribed antipsychotics were significantly more likely to have negative symptoms, which it also shows predicts not working. The authors address this seriously, with separate analyses controlling for prognostic potential (Vaillant), premorbid developmental achievement (Zigler), psychosis and negative symptoms, and a GEE logistic and proportional-odds model adjusting for prognosis, premorbid functioning and symptoms. Those adjustments are post-hoc, use dichotomised covariates, and cannot address baseline severity determining both medication continuation and work capacity. The specific 20-year comparison reported as 9/36 v. 16/22 is unadjusted.

old: A monocentre parallel-group trial with participants 'randomly assigned' and raters blinded to allocation, registered as DRKS00018107. Three things are missing or wrong. No method of sequence generation or allocation concealment is described anywhere. The trial registration postdates the start of recruitment (recruitment began August 2017; the DRKS identifier is a 2019 registration), so allocation cannot be said to have been concealed on the registry's evidence. And the CONSORT flow does not reconcile: 502 were assessed and 369 found not eligible, which leaves 133, but the box reads 'Eligible for randomization (n = 119)', and 119 minus the 23 not randomised is 96 rather than the 110 shown as randomised. Every step from 110 downwards does reconcile (56 and 54 allocated, 8 lost before T0 in each arm, 2 excluded from each, 46 and 44 analysed), so the outcome denominators are unaffected. Baseline PANSS negative scores differ appreciably (11.4 IPS versus 13.7 TAU).
new: Random allocation is stated, but sequence generation and allocation concealment are unreported in both article and registry. DRKS00018107 was registered retrospectively on 21 January 2021, after recruitment began 23 August 2017; the identifier does not establish a 2019 registration. Retrospective registration cannot establish allocation concealment either way. Figure 1 is inconsistent upstream (502-369=133 rather than 119; 133-23=110), but the 110 randomised and 56/54 allocated counts reconcile. Baseline negative-symptom imbalance and missing randomisation details support some concerns. Independent AI verification; does not satisfy a named human/non-author verification requirement. old: A monocentre parallel-group trial with participants 'randomly assigned' and raters blinded to allocation, registered as DRKS00018107. Three things are missing or wrong. No method of sequence generation or allocation concealment is described anywhere. The trial registration postdates the start of recruitment (recruitment began August 2017; the DRKS identifier is a 2019 registration), so allocation cannot be said to have been concealed on the registry's evidence. And the CONSORT flow does not reconcile: 502 were assessed and 369 found not eligible, which leaves 133, but the box reads 'Eligible for randomization (n = 119)', and 119 minus the 23 not randomised is 96 rather than the 110 shown as randomised. Every step from 110 downwards does reconcile (56 and 54 allocated, 8 lost before T0 in each arm, 2 excluded from each, 46 and 44 analysed), so the outcome denominators are unaffected. Baseline PANSS negative scores differ appreciably (11.4 IPS versus 13.7 TAU).
new: Random allocation is stated, but sequence generation and allocation concealment are unreported in both article and registry. DRKS00018107 was registered retrospectively on 21 January 2021, after recruitment began 23 August 2017; the identifier does not establish a 2019 registration. Retrospective registration cannot establish allocation concealment either way. Figure 1 is inconsistent upstream (502-369=133 rather than 119; 133-23=110), but the 110 randomised and 56/54 allocated counts reconcile. Baseline negative-symptom imbalance and missing randomisation details support some concerns. Independent AI verification; does not satisfy a named human/non-author verification requirement. old: Raised to high for this result specifically. This is the result whose duration threshold the report contradicts itself about: Table 2 calls it 'EET at least one day' and the Abstract calls it EET 'for at least 1 week'. The counts are stable across both statements, so what is at risk is not the number but what the number counts, and a one-day and a one-week threshold are different outcomes. The outcome is objectively defined (a competitive job held for at least one day at or above the minimum wage, or mainstream education leading to a recognised qualification) and 'the raters for assessments were blinded to the group allocation'. Two concerns remain. The IPS specialists themselves recorded contacts and were the route through which IPS participants entered jobs and courses, so ascertainment in the intervention arm ran partly through the people delivering it. And the measured construct is not stably defined across the report: Table 2 labels a row 'EET at least one day' while the Abstract describes the same counts as EET 'for at least 1 week'.

These raise some concerns; a text definition conflict alone does not establish intervention-dependent misclassification or likely substantial measurement bias sufficient for high. old: Registration postdates the start of recruitment, and no protocol or analysis plan is cited, so no prespecified analysis set can be checked. The primary outcome is stated inconsistently: 'EET at least 15 h per week for at least 1 week in the follow-up' in the Abstract, 'the percentage in EET for at least 15 h per week and for at least 1 week' in the aims, and 'the number of patients in EET (at least 15 h per week) that would lead to a nationally recognized vocational qualification or degree' in the analysis section, which describes only the education limb. Most seriously for a review of employment, the trial reports no arm-level competitive-employment count at any timepoint despite competitive employment being the intervention's target: the employment subgroup is given as a chi-square, p value, odds ratio and confidence interval with no numerators, and monthly EET rates appear only as a figure.
new: Official DRKS00018107 was retrospectively registered 21 January 2021 and names a 12-month employment/mainstream education outcome, but no dated preanalysis plan is available. Article definitions differ in duration and 15 hour threshold presentation, creating possible multiplicity/selection concern. These facts do not establish that the extracted EET result was chosen because of its effect estimate. Absence of separate arm-level competitive-job counts concerns missing employment evidence, not proof of biased selection of this EET result. Some concerns is supported; a categorical high judgement is not established. Independent AI verification; does not satisfy a named human/non-author verification requirement. old: Registration postdates the start of recruitment, and no protocol or analysis plan is cited, so no prespecified analysis set can be checked. The primary outcome is stated inconsistently: 'EET at least 15 h per week for at least 1 week in the follow-up' in the Abstract, 'the percentage in EET for at least 15 h per week and for at least 1 week' in the aims, and 'the number of patients in EET (at least 15 h per week) that would lead to a nationally recognized vocational qualification or degree' in the analysis section, which describes only the education limb. Most seriously for a review of employment, the trial reports no arm-level competitive-employment count at any timepoint despite competitive employment being the intervention's target: the employment subgroup is given as a chi-square, p value, odds ratio and confidence interval with no numerators, and monthly EET rates appear only as a figure.
new: Official DRKS00018107 was retrospectively registered 21 January 2021 and names a 12-month employment/mainstream education outcome, but no dated preanalysis plan is available. Article definitions differ in duration and 15 hour threshold presentation, creating possible multiplicity/selection concern. These facts do not establish that the extracted EET result was chosen because of its effect estimate. Absence of separate arm-level competitive-job counts concerns missing employment evidence, not proof of biased selection of this EET result. Some concerns is supported; a categorical high judgement is not established. Independent AI verification; does not satisfy a named human/non-author verification requirement. Applicability: these stored arm-specific counts are not themselves a comparative effect estimate; tool judgement applies provisionally to the source comparison and cannot certify whole-cohort prevalence eligibility.
